mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Urcaguary ‌place ​underworld jewels ​at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

Urcaguary ​appears ‌in ​incan tradition ‌as ​underworld ​jewels. The ​name's ​meaning, ​"He of ‌the ​underground", shapes ‌the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ‌Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ‌Urcaguary ​in ​ritual, text, ‌and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived ​into the ‌modern ​scholarly record.

‌The ​myths ​of Urcaguary ​survive ​in ‌fragments, summaries, ‌and ​later ‌retellings. Each ​version ​reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ‌— ​poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Urcaguary ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

overview.body:
**Urcaguary** ​(*urcaguary*) — ‌Underworld Jewels ‌· He ​of ​the underground ​— belongs ​to the ​Incan ‌tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Underworld ‌Jewels". The ​name means ‌"He of ​the ​underground"[^1].

**Urcaguary** ​is the ​Inca guardian ​of ‌what lies ​beneath the ‌mountains: gold, ​silver, ‌emeralds and ​the other ‌precious things ​sealed ‌in the ​earth. The ​figure is ‌known only ‌through ‌the colonial ​chronicle tradition ​and later ‌folklore, ​and the ​sources are ‌late, brief ​and ​partly modern ‌— but ​they agree ‌on ​the core: ​the underground ​hoard has ​a ‌watcher, and ‌it is ​not a ‌vault, ​it is ​a god.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly ‌spelling **Urcaguary** ​and serves ‌its temple ​at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/urcaguary/). ​The displayed ‌form is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description computed ‌from the ​displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*urcaguary* ‌contains the ​same letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics or ‌special ‌encoding is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Urcaguary** matches ​the ​conventional scholarly ‌romanization. ​The plain ‌ASCII ​form *urcaguary* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters, so ​no ‌lost diacritics ​or ​encoding transition ‌is ‌claimed. The ‌editorial ​work is ​to ‌fix one ​reviewed reference ​spelling, ‌preserve capitalization ​and ​provenance, and ‌keep ​the original ‌evidence ​visible. The ​displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a ‌description computed ​from ‌the displayed ​form ​itself.

meditation.body: What ​does it ‌mean ‌that a ​civilization gave ​its ​wealth a ​god? ​The Greeks ‌gave ​Hermes to ​commerce ‌and the ​Romans gave ‌Juno ​Moneta to ‌the ​mint; the ​Inca ​gave Urcaguary ​to ​gold that ‌was still ​in ‌the earth. ​That ‌choice contains ​a ‌complete economics. ​Gold's ‌natural place, ​the figure ​says, ‌is inside ‌the ‌mountain, where ​it ​is sacred; ‌extraction ​is not ​sin but ‌negotiation, ​and the ​negotiation ‌never ends, ​because ‌ownership never ​begins. ​The serpent ​with the ​deer's ‌head is ‌posted ​at a ‌boundary ​the modern ​world ‌refuses to ‌see — ‌the ‌line between ​the ‌surface we ​live ​on and ​the ‌interior we ​dig into. ​Every ​blast re-asks ‌his ​question in ​dynamite ​grammar: did ‌you ​ask, or ‌did you ​only ‌take? A ​civilization ‌that must ‌give ​its minerals ​a ​guardian has ​admitted something ‌the ‌ledger never ​records.[^1]
